To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the predictive skill of a conceptual rainfall-runoff model decreases in some catchments under climate change, but not in others.

(1) model predictive skill only declines when catchment processes change due to changing climatic drivers; (2) model predictive skill is unaffected when catchment processes do not change; (3) catchment processes change in response to prolonged periods of dry weather; and (4) catchments that experience prolonged dry periods are likely to be underrepresented in current runoff projections
conceptual rainfall-runoff model projections of runoff under changed climatic conditions are biased in catchments where climate-induced shifts in the rainfall-runoff processes are significant.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question whether rainfall-runoff models can be used to project future runoff under changed climatic conditions.
the question: How can we improve the accuracy of hydrological models when projecting runoff in response to climate change?
climate change impacts and the ability of rainfall-runoff models to simulate runoff changes under changing climatic drivers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
model performance is not necessarily biased in the face of climate change but that it can be.
the bias in the runoff projections due to climate induced shift in catchment response is dependent on the type of climate change and catchment type.
the model bias in the projected runoff is due to the change in catchment response to rainfall.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
model predictive skill only decreases when a catchment’s rainfall-runoff processes are altered by climate change.
climate change impact assessments based on rainfall-runoff models may be biased when the catchment's response to changed climate conditions is not taken into account.
climate change will not only affect runoff through changes in precipitation, but also through changes in catchment response, which is often overlooked in climate impact assessments.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the predictive skill of a rainfall-runoff model is not only determined by the model's structure and the quality of its parameterization, but also by the climatic conditions under which it is applied.
the capacity of conceptual rainfall-runoff to extrapolate is limited and that climate change impact on hydrological response needs to be considered in the model development and application.
climate-induced shifts in the catchment's response to rainfall need to be considered when projecting runoff under climate change.
